parts:
Not really, according to that example, it's p that must be constant, where p is the probability of sucess of the usual negative binomial parameterization of undergraduate courses, here I'll call it neg_binomial_undergrad (it doesn't exist on Stan, of course).

Then if you have something like:

y[1] ~ neg_binomial_undergrad(p, phi1)

y[2] ~ neg_binomial_undergrad(p, phi2)

Then:

(y[1] + y[2]) ~ neg_binomial_undergrad(p, phi1 + phi2)


On Stan neg_binomial_2, you'll have to use the fact that:

mu = p * phi/ (1 - p)

Then, you have:

y[1] ~ neg_binomial_2(p * phi1/ (1 - p), phi1)

y[2] ~ neg_binomial_2(p * phi2/ (1 - p), phi2)

(y[1] + y[2]) ~ neg_binomial_2(p * (phi1 + phi2)/ (1 - p), phi1 + phi2)


Not that useful, but as I said there might be other special cases of sum of independent negative binomial random variables that gives another negative binomial that I'm not aware of.

A quick test to check the results on R:

p = .4
phi1 = 11.5
phi2 = 4.6
first_ = rnbinom(1e6, phi1, mu=p * phi1/ (1 - p)) + rnbinom(1e4, phi2, mu=p * phi2/ (1 - p))
second_ = rnbinom(1e6, phi1 + phi2, mu=p * (phi1 + phi2)/ (1 - p))
mean(first_)
mean(second_)
var(first_)
var(second_)
mean(first_**3)
mean(second_**3)
quantile(first_)
quantile(second_)
